summary.text: A system of linear equations is a collection of two or more linear equations involving the same variables.
A solution assigns values to the variables so that all the equations are satisfied simultaneously.
With two variables each equation determines a line, so the solution set is where the lines meet: a line, a single point, or the empty set.

facts.value: (x, y, z) = (1, −2, −2) fits all three equations

facts.label: Two variables
facts.value: Each equation determines a line on the xy-plane

facts.label: Three variables
facts.value: Each equation determines a plane in three-dimensional space

items.prompt: Three flat sheets are all parallel and sit apart from one another. What can you say about the solution set of their three equations?

options.label: It is one single common point
It is a whole line of points
It is empty, no shared point
It is a whole plane of points

items.explain: Three parallel planes do not have a common point, so the solution set of their equations is empty.

items.prompt: Two equations in x and y draw two lines that cross at one spot. How many solutions does the system have?

options.label: Exactly one, where they cross
Infinitely many, all along both
None, since they never agree
Two, one for each of the lines

items.explain: The solution set is the intersection of the lines, and two lines crossing share a single unique point.

items.prompt: A system has fewer equations than unknowns. In general, what should you expect?

options.label: Exactly one unique solution
Infinitely many, or possibly none
Exactly two separate solutions
Never any solutions at all

items.explain: In general such an underdetermined system has infinitely many solutions, but it may have no solution.

items.prompt: A system has more equations than unknowns. In general, what should you expect?

options.label: No solution
Exactly one solution
Infinitely many solutions
A solution for every choice of values

items.explain: In general a system with more equations than unknowns has no solution; it is called overdetermined.

items.prompt: Someone finds values that satisfy two of the three equations in a system. Have they found a solution of the system?

options.label: Yes, satisfying most of them is enough
Yes, as long as the two are linear
No, every equation must hold at once
Only if the third is non-linear

items.explain: A solution must make all the equations simultaneously satisfied.

items.prompt: Three equations in two unknowns draw three lines. Under which condition can the system still be solved?

options.label: Never, since extra equations always rule it out
Only when two of the lines are parallel
Only when the lines never touch
When all three lines meet at a single point

items.explain: A system of three equations and two unknowns can be solvable if the three lines intersect at a single point.

beats.title: Where the lines meet
beats.hook: One equation leaves plenty of room; stack on more and that room can shrink to a point or vanish.

beats.prompt: Two equations in x and y draw two parallel lines. What is the solution set?
beats.explain: It is possible for a system of two equations and two unknowns to have no solution, if the two lines are parallel.

choices.label: One point
choices.feedback: Parallel lines never cross, so there is no single meeting point.

choices.label: A whole line
choices.feedback: That needs the two lines to coincide, which parallel lines do not.

beats.prompt: match each number of variables to what one equation draws
beats.explain: Each linear equation determines a flat shape one dimension below the space of its variables, and the solution set is their intersection.

beats.prompt: A system has the same number of equations as unknowns. In general, what do you expect?
beats.explain: In general, a system with the same number of equations and unknowns has a single unique solution.

choices.label: No solution
choices.feedback: That is the usual outcome with more equations than unknowns, not with equal numbers.

choices.label: Infinitely many solutions
choices.feedback: That is the usual outcome with fewer equations than unknowns.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Each of three equations in three variables determines a plane.
The solution set is the intersection of the three planes.
Three planes can meet at a single point, which gives one solution.
So the solution set of three planes can never be a line.

beats.explain: The solution set may be a plane, a line, a single point, or the empty set; three planes passing through two points share the whole line through them.

beats.idea: A solution must satisfy every equation together, so the solution set is where all their lines or planes intersect.

paragraphs.heading: Several equations at once
paragraphs.text: A linear system is a set of two or more linear equations that all use the same variables. A solution gives a value to each variable so that every equation holds at the same moment. The collection of all such solutions is called the solution set. A lone equation such as 2x = 4 has the answer x = 2, but most interesting systems have two equations or more.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Linear systems are a basic building block of linear algebra, which most modern mathematics uses. Methods for solving them by computer belong to numerical linear algebra and play a big part in engineering, physics, chemistry, computer science and economics. Even a nonlinear system can often be approximated by a linear one, a trick called linearization, which helps when building a model or simulation of something complicated.

paragraphs.heading: Lines and planes
paragraphs.text: With two variables, x and y, each equation draws a line on the xy-plane. Since a solution must satisfy every equation, the solution set is where the lines meet: a whole line, a single point, or nothing. With three variables each equation is a plane in space, and the answer can be a plane, a line, a point or empty. Three parallel planes, for example, share no point, so their system has no solution.

paragraphs.heading: Counting equations and unknowns
paragraphs.text: Usually the number of equations compared with the number of unknowns decides how a system behaves. With fewer equations than unknowns there are typically infinitely many solutions, though there may be none; this is an underdetermined system. With equal numbers there is typically exactly one solution. With more equations than unknowns there is typically no solution; this is an overdetermined system.

paragraphs.heading: The exceptions
paragraphs.text: These rules describe the general case, and particular values of the coefficients can break them. Two equations in two unknowns have no solution if their lines are parallel. Three equations in two unknowns can still be solved if all three lines pass through one point.

paragraphs.heading: The matrix form
paragraphs.text: A vector equation can be traded for an equivalent matrix equation, A𝐱 = 𝐛. In it, A is an m×n matrix, while 𝐱 and 𝐛 are columns holding n and m entries respectively. The coefficients and unknowns are often real or complex numbers, but integers, rational numbers and polynomials appear too.
